title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
summary:
As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’

Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, as he joined Silicon Valley heavyweights in demanding the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.
The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.

“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia.
“He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return,” Trump said.

Trump’s comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that are in turn supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang, who resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Days before, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife.

Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration.
The letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged spy and another with a subordinate.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.
One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”.

Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress – the best option.
“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.

Meanwhile, the US government has also introduced new restrictions on chip sales designed to stop the technology being diverted to countries such as China.

The new rule announced on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted.

“The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Commerce Department said.

Huang reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy who also worked as an executive at an Nvidia customer, Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed is under suspicion, according to reports, of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.

Megaspeeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Ms Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complies “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.
Nvidia shares opened down 2.7% on Monday, knocking about $100bn (£75.8bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82tn.
